source.title: Embedding Principle in Depth for the Loss Landscape Analysis of Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Zhiwei Bai; Tao Luo; Z. Xu; Yaoyu Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The supplied text gives inconsistent publication dates: the header says June 2024, while the arXiv line says 14 Apr 2025.
record.tranche_reason: Reports held-out accuracy before and after pruning layers, and train/test accuracy at a training plateau. These bear on generalization under depth changes but do not test any listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports training-loss and layer-linearization outcomes for batch normalization, larger datasets, and different depths. Those do not measure a train/test generalization gap, so they are not rows. Cited findings from prior work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests depth-wise critical-point embedding and layer pruning, not any listed claim version. Its held-out accuracy results do not test random-label memorization, width scaling, architectural comparisons, optimizers, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors establish a depth-wise embedding principle and present proof-of-concept experiments on shared training dynamics, increased critical-point degeneracy, optimization benefits of batch normalization and larger datasets, and layer pruning. They argue that the resulting landscape hierarchy helps explain similarities in training and generalization across network sizes, while calling for systematic experimental validation.
record.recipe_differences: Studies critical-point lifting and layer pruning in depth, rather than the random-label, optimizer, batch-size, regularization, sharpness, or memorized-example procedures in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scale and training-set size affect layer linearization; batch-normalization scale affects layer linearization and training stagnation. These outcomes concern training dynamics, not measured generalization gaps.

fits_no_version.finding: At a shared Iris training plateau, one- and three-hidden-layer networks attain 66.7% training and test accuracy and entirely misclassify one class.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With small initialization, networks of different depths can encounter plateaus with similar training and held-out performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Merging five effectively linear layers of a ten-hidden-layer MNIST network and additionally training the reduced network yields 95.27% test accuracy versus 95.4% originally, with approximately 98.54% prediction agreement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning effectively linear layers followed by additional training can approximately preserve held-out accuracy in the reported MNIST example.

record.problems: The experiments are described as proofs of concept. The Iris result is a plateau case study, and the MNIST pruning comparison does not report uncertainty or a control pruning comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted for the training-loss or MPC traces in Figures 3, 6, and 7, or the Fashion-MNIST MPC sweep in Figure B3, because these do not report the generalization measure named by the claim. Hessian eigenvalue results in Figure 5 measure degeneracy, not the listed gap measure. Cited prior-work results were excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance compared with natural-label training.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error across data sizes and regularization settings.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps; Hessian degeneracy does not measure this relationship.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized training examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The June 2024 journal publication date and April 2025 arXiv revision date need not conflict. Neither generalization discussion nor the cited original findings establish a test of V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test random-label memorization or compare random-label and natural-label generalization.
Does not sweep width past the interpolation threshold or measure test error against width.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected image classifiers.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD for held-out performance.
Does not test batch-size effects on held-out performance.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with the generalization gap.
Does not remove memorized examples or measure the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer NN
rows.stage_stated: trained with full-batch gradient descent; learning rate 0.01 for the 1-D experiments
rows.operation_detail: Measured training accuracy at the shared plateau with the three-hidden-layer network.
rows.note: The study reports this accuracy for both networks at the plateau but does not give a training-versus-test gap comparison as a result.
rows.check: The 66.7% Iris training accuracy is supported but measures no listed version. The stated learning rate of 0.01 applies to the specified 1-D experiments, not explicitly to Figure 4; remove that attribution.

rows.subject: three-hidden-layer NN
rows.stage_stated: trained with full-batch gradient descent; learning rate 0.01 for the 1-D experiments
rows.operation_detail: Measured test accuracy at the shared plateau with the single-hidden-layer network.
rows.note: The study states that both networks have nearly the same training and test accuracy and that both completely misclassify one of the three classes.
rows.check: The 66.7% Iris test accuracy is supported but measures no listed version. The stated learning rate of 0.01 is not explicitly specified for Figure 4.

rows.subject: 10-hidden-layer network
rows.stage_stated: trained with stochastic gradient descent, batch size 1000, learning rate 0.001, for 100 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Pruned five effectively linear layers by merging their weights.
rows.note: The authors describe the reduced model's generalization performance as approximately preserved.
rows.check: Change partial to cannot_determine because no listed version concerns layer pruning. The evaluated subject is the pruned five-hidden-layer network, and the comparison follows additional training after pruning; 95.27% versus 95.4% is not an immediate pruning-only effect.

rows.subject: 10-hidden-layer network and pruned 5-hidden-layer network
rows.size_stated: width 50 for each hidden layer before pruning
rows.stage_stated: trained with stochastic gradient descent, batch size 1000, learning rate 0.001, for 100 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Compared model predictions on the test set before and after pruning.
rows.note: The result compares predictions across models, not accuracy against chance.
rows.check: The approximately 98.54% prediction agreement is supported but measures no listed version. Specify that the pruned network was additionally trained before comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
